blocks.text: A place to store a piece of data

A station has six helmets available. If the program needs to use this quantity several times, it can store it in an object. Here, an object means a region of memory associated with data; we are not yet talking about classes or object-oriented programming. Its type determines what kinds of values and operations the object supports.

A variable gives that object a name. In int cascos = 6, int indicates the integer type, cascos is the name chosen for the variable, and 6 is its initial value. An integer represents a quantity without a fractional part, within a finite range. Using cascos later lets us access the stored value without repeating the number in every statement.
The output is 6. The output statement receives the value of the variable: it does not print the name cascos. The name belongs to the code we read; the value is the data the program works with.
Distinguishing name, type, and value

Think of a box with a label. The label cascos lets us identify it; the designation int tells us what it can contain; 6 is its current content. This comparison helps us follow programs, but does not mean we must draw the exact physical storage. Each object exists according to its type's rules.

blocks.question: In int visitantes = 14;, what does visitantes represent?
options: The name used to refer to the object.
blocks.explanation: int is the type, visitantes is the name, and 14 is the initial value.

blocks.text: Reading data does not change it
The same variable can appear several times as output data. Reading its value does not erase or reduce it. In the following program, no statement changes what botellas contains.

blocks.explanation: The string literal prints a written label; the variable prints its value.

blocks.question: Why do two reads of the same variable produce the same value when nothing changes it?
options: Every output statement creates a different variable.
The second output statement retrieves text from the first message.
The value is preserved between statements.
blocks.explanation: Memory retains the data; cout receives its value rather than somehow replaying an earlier output.

blocks.text: Choosing a representation

Not all data represents whole-number quantities. A length of 1.25 meters requires a numerical representation that supports fractions; a label such as Sector 4 is text, even though it contains a digit; a yes-or-no response can be represented by a Boolean value. We will study these representations in the coming lessons. Choosing a type starts with understanding what the data means, not just looking for digits.

blocks.question: A program must add up the number of tables in two rooms. What representation fits the number of tables?
options: A character containing the first letter of the name.
An integer that counts the tables.
blocks.explanation: Counting complete objects requires a whole-number quantity; text may describe it but does not serve the same purpose.

blocks.question: A box identifier is 0042, and its two leading zeros must be preserved. What do we need to represent?
blocks.explanation: 0042 is an identifier. Preserving its characters matters more than treating it as a quantity.

blocks.text: A type restricts the operations and values that are possible. It does not, by itself, verify that the data correctly describes the real world: a negative integer can be legal in C++ yet make no sense as a number of tables.
Build before comparing

In the lab, use the requirements to write a program that stores the number of keys in a workshop and displays Keys: 7. Use a variable named llaves with the value 7. Then change only its initial value to 11: the message should become Keys: 11 without changing the output statement. Predict both results before running the program.

Check the fixed text, the value, and the space between them separately. If the message does not change when the variable changes, check whether you printed a fixed number or the variable name inside quotation marks. The lab preserves your latest code draft when you reopen the lesson. If you want to compare several versions, save a separate copy of each one outside the editor.
One solution and a new reading
The variable stores the data, and the output statement uses it. Changing 7 to 11 in its definition changes its initial content; the same output statement still expresses the same purpose.

blocks.question: Recall what you learned about lines: what are the two exact output lines?
blocks.explanation: The first statement produces text and a newline. The second combines a value with explanatory text.

blocks.text: Reference solution: Number of keys
Consult this comparison after building and checking your own attempt. The reference shows one possible implementation; the criteria help you recognize other correct solutions.

Correctness criteria: the variable is named llaves and stores the integer 7; the output statement uses that variable. The output must be Keys: 7, with a space after the colon. Changing only its initial value to 11 must make the same statement produce Keys: 11. Equivalent forms of declaration and output are acceptable if they meet these conditions. In this reference, int llaves{7}; creates and initializes the integer llaves with the value 7, just like int llaves = 7; for this data.

Keys: is fixed text; llaves supplies the current value. Change {7} to {11} without changing the output statement. Always printing the literal 7 or the string "llaves" does not satisfy the experiment, even if the first output looks correct.
